FAQs 
 Overview
The Instron® 2810-005 Coefficient of Friction Fixture measures the static and kinetic coefficient of friction of plastic film and sheet, in accordance with ASTM D1894 and ISO 8295. A weighted sled is pulled across a fixed horizontal table while a load cell records the force required — giving you accurate, repeatable friction data your quality and R&D teams can trust.
The fixture mounts directly into your universal testing system using Instron's standard Type D base grip adapter, so you can add coefficient of friction testing to an existing frame without buying dedicated equipment.
 Benefits
Test your way — Mount the specimen to the sled, the table, or both, so you can match the fixture setup to your exact material and test requirements.
Start testing right away — Comes with both a nylon and a metal tow line included, so you're ready to test without sourcing additional parts.
Use the equipment you already have — Adaptable to most standard universal testing instruments, protecting your existing investment in test equipment.
 Applications
Plastic film and sheeting friction testing for quality control, incoming material inspection, and R&D
Tensile-mode coefficient of friction testing (not intended for high-rate/high-speed applications)
 How It Works
A tow line connects the sled to a low-force load cell, running over a guide pulley. As the crosshead moves, the sled is pulled across the table and the load cell records force throughout the test:
Static coefficient of friction is calculated from the first force peak on the load curve
Kinetic coefficient of friction is calculated from the average force between two defined points
Coefficient of friction = recorded force ÷ sled mass

 Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)
What testing standards does the 2810-005 support?Collapse
The Instron Coefficient of Friction Fixture is designed to test in accordance with ASTM D1894 and ISO 8295, the two most widely used standards for measuring static and kinetic coefficient of friction in plastic film and sheeting.
Will this fixture work with the testing system I already have?Expand
The fixture mounts using Instron's standard Type D base grip adapter and connects to the load cell via a Type C coupling, so it's adaptable to most standard universal testing instruments — not just Instron systems with matching fittings. Check with our applications team to confirm compatibility with your specific frame.
Can I test both sides of my material in one setup?Expand
Yes. The test specimen can be mounted to the sled, the table, or both, depending on what your standard or material requires — giving you flexibility to test film-on-film, film-on-metal, or other combinations.
Is this fixture suitable for high-speed friction testing?Expand
No — the 2810-005 is designed for tensile-mode (standard-speed) testing only and is not intended for high-rate or high-speed friction applications. If your application requires higher-speed testing, let us know and we can help identify the right alternative.
What is coefficient of friction testing and why does it matter for plastic film?Expand
Coefficient of friction (COF) testing measures how easily one surface slides against another — in this case, how easily plastic film or sheeting slides against itself or another material. It matters because friction affects how film behaves in real-world use: too much friction can cause jamming or tearing during high-speed packaging and manufacturing processes, while too little can cause slipping, poor stacking stability, or product mishandling. Manufacturers test COF to ensure film performs consistently on packaging lines, in shipping, and in end-use applications.
What's the difference between static and kinetic coefficient of friction?Expand
Static coefficient of friction measures the force needed to start moving one surface against another from a resting position — essentially, how much resistance there is to overcome before sliding begins. Kinetic (or dynamic) coefficient of friction measures the force needed to keep the surfaces moving once sliding has already started. Static friction is typically higher than kinetic friction, and both values matter for different reasons: static friction relates to how film behaves when stationary (like on a stack or roll), while kinetic friction relates to how it behaves once in motion (like running through packaging equipment).
What equipment do you need to test coefficient of friction on plastic film?Expand
At minimum, you need: a universal testing system (or equivalent frame) capable of controlled, constant-speed horizontal pulling; a coefficient of friction fixture, which includes a weighted sled and a flat test table or plate; a load cell sensitive enough to accurately capture low-force readings; and a tow line connecting the sled to the load cell. You'll also need testing software to run the test and calculate results — Instron's Bluehill® Universal software includes a pre-built ASTM D1894 test method, so you can start testing right out of the box or customize it to match your specific procedure.
